themes.briefing:
Two converging investigative findings from ProPublica illustrate how regulatory failures and ideologically driven medical refusals are imposing severe, preventable harm on American families. On the public health front, a national study of more than five million births found that the rate of newborns not receiving the vitamin K shot surged 77 percent between 2017 and 2024 — a trend almost certainly linked to anti-vaccine sentiment migrating to routine newborn care[28]. The consequences are not abstract: the CDC calculates that unvaccinated newborns are 81 times more likely to develop late vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a condition that causes spontaneous brain hemorrhage, and in virtually every reviewed case these deaths were preventable with a single prophylactic injection that has been standard pediatric practice for more than six decades[28]. Experts believe that hundreds of infant deaths annually may be attributable to this deficiency, yet the phenomenon remains largely untracked at the national level, compounding the difficulty of mounting a coordinated public health response.

A parallel failure of regulatory accountability is playing out in Oklahoma, where the Meredith family's newly constructed home was inundated with thick black oily sludge rising through the foundation in August 2025, apparently from an improperly plugged oil well drilled in the 1940s beneath the property[27]. When the family turned to the Oklahoma Corporation Commission — the agency statutorily responsible for overseeing oil and gas pollution and plugging abandoned wells — they were told the agency could not help them[27]. The episode exposes a structural gap of enormous scale: Oklahoma officially acknowledges approximately 19,000 orphan wells requiring remediation, but federal researchers estimate the actual number likely exceeds 300,000[27]. The Meredith case is therefore not an anomaly but a foreseeable consequence of chronic under-enforcement and under-resourced oversight in a state with a century of hydrocarbon extraction history. Taken together, these cases reflect a broader pattern in which the gap between nominal regulatory mandates and operational capacity leaves ordinary citizens bearing the full cost of systemic failures — whether in a doctor's office or beneath a home foundation.

references.title: Oily Sludge Is Flooding Their Dream Home. Oklahoma Regulators Say They Can't Help.
Tiny Footprints, a Blue Blanket: What I Can't Forget About the Babies Who Died of Vitamin K Deficiency

themes.briefing:
The American economy is exhibiting compounding structural stress across multiple fronts simultaneously. Consumer prices rose 3.8% year-over-year in April — the highest inflation reading in three years — while producer prices climbed 6% over the same period, and for the first time in three years, American wages are failing to keep pace with inflation[22]. This dynamic is politically significant: President Trump's approval rating on the economy has fallen below levels President Biden ever recorded, despite Trump having won reelection largely on promises to reduce prices[22]. The confluence of resurgent inflation and stagnant real wages signals that the reprieve consumers experienced from peak-cycle inflation has been short-lived, and the policy toolkit available to address it remains constrained.

Beneath the inflation headline lies a deeper structural shift in how Americans relate to debt. The country has moved from borrowing to build future productive capacity to borrowing simply to maintain current consumption[20]. This is visible at every level: the federal government is now servicing trillion-dollar annual interest payments, corporations are making leveraged bets on AI infrastructure, and consumers are increasingly financing everyday necessities — groceries, food delivery — through credit[20]. What was once a financing choice has effectively become a survival mechanism for a growing segment of the population, representing a qualitative change in the nature of American indebtedness rather than merely a quantitative one[20].

Markets face their own set of compounding vulnerabilities. Big Tech's advertising-dependent revenue models — Meta derives 97% of revenues from advertising, Google approximately 75% — render the sector acutely exposed to any sustained pullback in consumer spending that elevated inflation and debt servicing costs are likely to produce[22]. Meanwhile, speculative capital continues to flow into AI ventures, raising questions about whether certain high-profile entries represent durable value creation or a repeat of dot-com-era excess[22,23]. The broader picture is one of an economy where structural debt dependency, re-accelerating inflation, and asset market speculation are reinforcing one another in ways that constrain both household and policymaker flexibility going forward.

themes.briefing:
The physical costs of AI infrastructure are coming into sharp relief as large-scale projects move from planning documents into contested terrain. The approved $100 billion 'Stratos' project in Box Elder County, Utah — spanning roughly 40,000 acres near the Great Salt Lake basin — illustrates the scale of resource demands that AI buildout now imposes on local communities and ecosystems[25]. The project's potential energy draw of up to 9 gigawatts exceeds the entire current electricity consumption of the state of Utah, and nearly 4,000 formal complaints were lodged ahead of approval, citing water usage, air quality, and threats to the Great Salt Lake ecosystem[25]. The use of Utah's Military Installation Development Authority to advance the project raises a structurally important concern: that national security framing is being deployed as a mechanism to circumvent local environmental and democratic oversight — a pattern likely to recur as AI infrastructure competition intensifies[25].

The employment projections surrounding Stratos also warrant scrutiny. Project advocates, including investor Kevin O'Leary, have cited figures of 10,000 construction jobs and 2,000 permanent positions, while more measured reporting places those numbers at roughly 4,000 construction jobs over a decade and approximately 1,350 permanent roles[25]. This gap between promotional and analytical estimates is not incidental — it reflects a broader dynamic in which the economic case for transformative infrastructure is systematically overstated to offset environmental and community opposition. Policymakers evaluating similar proposals elsewhere should treat headline employment figures as opening bids rather than forecasts.

At the demand side of the AI ecosystem, the attention economy that drives consumer engagement with AI-powered platforms is itself becoming a subject of active resistance. Stanford educators and authors Bill Burnett and Dave Evans have engaged in public discourse — alongside commentators like Scott Galloway — around the mechanics of fighting algorithmic capture, building intentional digital habits, and reclaiming agency from platforms engineered to maximize time-on-screen[24]. While the conversation remains largely in the register of personal development, its underlying tension is structural: the same AI infrastructure being built at enormous physical and environmental cost in places like Utah is, at the consumer end, optimized to extract maximal attention from users. The supply chain of the attention economy now runs through contested desert ecosystems and strained power grids — a connection that mainstream technology discourse has yet to fully reckon with[24,25].

themes.theme: Trump Foreign Policy: Iran War, China & NATO
themes.briefing:
The Iran conflict is entering a precarious second phase as diplomatic efforts collapse. Iran has rejected U.S. demands and, according to Iran's semi-official Mehr news agency, offered 'no tangible concessions' while accusing Washington of the same — leaving the military option actively back on the table as Trump reportedly prepared to convene his national security team to discuss next steps[14]. The war itself, which began in late February, was already politically costly at the outset: approximately 48 percent of Americans opposed it from the start, a figure that has since climbed to nearly 60 percent opposition as of mid-May[10]. Energy markets are registering the strain, with U.S. East Coast diesel inventories running 11–18 percent below seasonal norms and European gas storage at roughly half its typical level for the period, indicators that a further shock from continued Strait of Hormuz disruption could have severe economic consequences[14]. Trump's public warning that 'the clock is ticking' for Iran, issued amid a global bond selloff, underscores how tightly the conflict's military and economic dimensions are now intertwined[14].

The Iran operation is simultaneously fracturing the NATO alliance in ways that could produce lasting strategic damage. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth halted a planned deployment of roughly 4,000 American troops to Poland and announced the withdrawal of an additional 5,000 troops from Europe — a decision that caught Pentagon officials off guard and appears directly linked to European allies' opposition to the Iran campaign[11]. This is strategically self-defeating: Poland currently spends close to 5 percent of GDP on defense and subsidizes the cost of American forces on its soil, while Romania, Bulgaria, Croatia, and the Baltic states have spent a decade building capable militaries specifically along the eastern flank hardened against Russian aggression[11]. Managing alliance relationships through punitive troop withdrawals in response to allied disagreement treats democratic partners — who must operate within their own constitutional processes — as subordinates rather than strategic assets, undermining the very platform that projects American power in Eurasia[11].

On China, the administration's strategic incoherence is equally pronounced. The prevailing Washington consensus that Trump was 'right about China' is analytically weak: his first term prioritized soybean sales and praised Beijing's Covid response to court bilateral trade, and his second term continues to measure success by commodity export volumes rather than geopolitical positioning[12]. The Obama-era Trans-Pacific Partnership, abandoned by Trump, represented a more coherent framework — combining trade economics with a coalition-based posture of skepticism toward Chinese power[12]. Expert observers such as Stephen Roach, a senior scholar at Yale's Paul Tsai China Center and former Morgan Stanley Asia chairman, have long argued that U.S.-China relations are defined by deep structural codependency that simplistic tariff strategies cannot resolve[13]. Trump's pattern of granting favorable treatment to Nvidia on export controls while fixating on bilateral trade deficits reflects an administration that mistakes mercantilist bookkeeping for geopolitical competition — and one constitutionally incapable of assembling the coalition of liberal democracies that serious strategic rivalry with China would require[12].

themes.theme: Supreme Court, Rule of Law & Electoral Integrity
themes.briefing:
The Supreme Court's docket and shadow docket activity this week carry significant implications for electoral integrity and voting rights. The Court's 6-3 decision in Louisiana v. Callais has substantially narrowed the reach of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, and the justices have now remanded at least two additional VRA cases back to lower courts in its wake — a move that drew a sharp dissent from Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, who argued the remanded cases presented a distinct question of Section 2's private enforceability that the Callais ruling did not resolve[17]. Separately, the Court declined to reinstate Virginia's new congressional map ahead of the 2026 elections, a decision that prompted Governor Abigail Spanberger to publicly accuse the Court of nullifying an election and the votes of more than three million Virginians — rhetoric that, while politically charged, reflects mounting institutional tension over the judiciary's role in shaping electoral outcomes[19].

Within the Court itself, an ideological fault line is sharpening in ways that may prove consequential for future rulings. Justice Neil Gorsuch's public advocacy for a 'creedal' vision of American identity — grounding citizenship in shared ideals rather than ethnicity or lineage — has drawn fierce backlash from hard-right nativist commentators who view originalists like Gorsuch, Barrett, and Roberts as insufficiently committed to an ethno-cultural conception of the American founding[16]. This internal fracture on the right is not merely academic: the tension between originalist jurisprudence and nativist ideology is likely to surface in pending rulings on birthright citizenship and related questions, where the Court's textualist wing may reach conclusions that disappoint its most aggressive political supporters[16]. SCOTUSblog's historical survey of ideologically 'strange bedfellows' on the Court — noting, for instance, that the 'conservative' Justice Harlan II was more willing than the 'progressive' Justice Black to invalidate state intrusions on personal liberty in Griswold v. Connecticut — reinforces that judicial alignments resist simple partisan mapping and that principled legal reasoning can diverge sharply from political expectation[18].

On the electoral integrity front, the case of Tina Peters — the Colorado county clerk convicted for tampering with election machinery she claimed was compromised — illustrates the downstream legal and institutional damage wrought by election denialism. Peters disabled security cameras monitoring election equipment and granted unauthorized access to the machines, yet Colorado's 2020 results in Mesa County tracked closely with 2016 patterns, analytically undermining her fraud claims at their foundation[15]. Colorado Governor Jared Polis's decision to commute her sentence adds a further layer of complexity, raising questions about accountability norms for elected officials who abuse their positions in pursuit of conspiratorial narratives[15]. Taken together, the week's developments — VRA erosion, redistricting disputes, and the normalization of election-integrity misconduct — present a compounding challenge to the institutional frameworks designed to ensure free and fair elections.

themes.briefing:
Donald Trump's political standing has deteriorated markedly entering the late spring of 2026. His net approval rating hit a second-term low of -20.1 as of mid-May, a steady slide from -18.6 two weeks prior, with individual pollsters registering net ratings as low as -26 (CBS News/YouGov)[1]. Approval on economic management is especially toxic: net approval on inflation and cost of living stands at -41.8, while his general economic net approval reached a new low of -27.4[1]. Translated into raw sentiment, CBS News/YouGov finds only 20% of Americans strongly approve of Trump while 52% strongly disapprove, and 51% of the public says he does not care at all about people like them[6]. Analyst Ron Brownstein's assessment — that Trump is in a deeper hole than any recent president heading into a midterm — is borne out by the trajectory: his approval has fallen from 41% in January 2026 to 37% in May, with disapproval rising from 59% to 63% over the same period[6].

The structural implications for the 2026 midterms are significant. The Silver Bulletin generic congressional ballot average now stands at D +6.6, the highest point of the current cycle[2]. That figure is nearly identical to the D +6.8 reading at the equivalent moment in the 2018 cycle, when Democrats ultimately picked up 40 House seats[2]. Individual polls have registered even more dramatic leads — AtlasIntel at D +14 and NYT/Siena at D +11 — though the Silver Bulletin average applies methodological corrections for house effects and polling frequency[2]. The Republican Party's deep organizational identification with Trump amplifies this exposure: because the GOP has so thoroughly branded itself around the president, his personal unpopularity functions as a direct electoral liability for congressional candidates[6].

Beyond the polling numbers, two emerging narratives risk compounding Trump's political difficulties. The first is a perception of personal corruption: reporting documents that Trump purchased Nvidia stock shortly before a Commerce Department ruling allowing chip sales to China, bought Palantir shares days before a major DHS contract award, and acquired Axon stock coinciding with a large ICE taser purchase — a pattern that observers argue reflects systematic self-dealing[7]. The second concerns Trump's fitness for office. Physical indicators — including visible swelling in his ankles, apparent episodes of falling asleep during televised events, multiple unexplained medical appointments, and the concealment of hand discoloration with heavy makeup — have drawn commentary[9], though Democrats have largely refrained from making his health a public line of attack, with neither the DSCC nor the DCCC engaging the issue on social media[9]. Bill Kristol argues that voters are now internalizing the view that Trump governs primarily for himself rather than for their interests[3], a dynamic that, if it consolidates, would reinforce the midterm environment already suggested by the generic ballot data.

big_picture:
The dominant thread running through today's intelligence digest is the convergence of self-inflicted institutional failures across domestic governance, economic management, and geopolitical strategy — each compounding the others in ways that are now registering in measurable public backlash. The Trump administration's political standing has deteriorated to historic lows, with a net approval of -20.1 and economic net approval at -27.4[1], driven by an inflation rate of 3.8% year-over-year and producer prices at 6% — the first period in three years where wages are failing to keep pace[22]. These numbers are not occurring in isolation: they are the downstream consequence of policy choices, from tariff structures to regulatory rollbacks, that are now visible to ordinary Americans at the grocery store and the gas pump. Meanwhile, regulatory failures in public health — most starkly illustrated by the 77% surge in newborns not receiving vitamin K shots[28] — and a Supreme Court systematically narrowing the Voting Rights Act[5] suggest that the institutional decay is not limited to economic management but extends across the state's basic protective functions.

The geopolitical and technological dimensions of today's briefings reveal a second compounding layer: the United States is simultaneously prosecuting an active and politically costly war with Iran[14], managing a fraught strategic competition with China, and attempting to anchor a $100 billion AI infrastructure buildout that would draw up to 9 gigawatts of power near the already-stressed Great Salt Lake basin[25]. These are not separable crises. The Iran conflict consumes diplomatic bandwidth and military resources at precisely the moment when AI infrastructure investment requires stable international supply chains, reliable energy policy, and long-term regulatory coherence — none of which the current environment provides. The Stratos project's energy demands alone exceed the consumption of entire mid-sized nations, and its approval without apparent resolution of water and grid stress signals that the federal government is layering future liabilities onto an already strained system.

Taken together, today's briefings describe a polity under compressive stress from multiple directions at once. The Supreme Court's retrenchment on voting rights[5], falling real wages[22], active military conflict[14], and the erosion of routine public health infrastructure[28] are all occurring against a backdrop of a president whose approval on the core metric of economic management sits at -41.8 on cost of living[1] — numbers that historically correlate with severe midterm losses. The 2026 midterm environment is being shaped not by any single policy failure but by the accumulated weight of simultaneous breakdowns in the state's capacity to protect, stabilize, and project power credibly. Whether any one of these threads might be managed in isolation is now largely a moot question; the interaction effects between them are what define the current strategic moment.
